extracted.intended_audience: Students and practitioners building a machine-learning career and learning to read research papers
extracted.subtask_short: Andrew Ng's advice on reading ML research papers
extracted.subtask_description: A KDnuggets summary of Andrew Ng's CS230 lecture on efficient strategies for reading machine-learning research papers and navigating a career in ML. Each item is a recommended strategy or quality the reader should apply when engaging with a paper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compile a list of papers to read
rubrics_metrics.description: Compile a list of papers: try to create a list of research papers, medium posts and whatever text or learning resource you have.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Starting point for systematic reading; the list should aggregate research papers and other learning resources on the topic of interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skip around the list and read papers in parallel
rubrics_metrics.description: Skip around the list: basically, you should read research papers in a parallel fashion; meaning try to tackle more than one paper at a time. Concretely, try to quickly skim and understand each of these paper and do not read it all, maybe you read 10-20% of each one and probably that will be enough to give you a high-level understanding of the paper in hand. After that, you may decide to eliminate some of these papers or just go over one or two them and read them fully.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reading 5-20 papers in a field may be enough to implement a system but not enough to be at the cutting-edge. Reading 50-100 papers gives you a very good understanding of the domain application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Take multiple passes through each paper
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't start reading the paper from the first to the last word. Instead, take multiple passes through the paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multi-pass reading is the recommended technique; do not read linearly from first word to last word.

rubrics_metrics.name: First pass: title, abstract, figures
rubrics_metrics.description: Read the Title, the abstract and the figures: by reading the title, abstract, the key network architecture figure, and maybe the experiments section, you will be able to get a general sense of the concepts in the paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In deep learning, there are a lot of research papers where the entire paper is summarized in one or two figures without the need to go hardly through the text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Second pass: introduction, conclusions, figures; skim the rest
rubrics_metrics.description: Read the introduction + conclusions + figures + skim the rest: the introduction, the conclusions and the abstract are the places where the author(s) try to summarize their work carefully to clarify for the reviewer why their paper should be accepted for publication. Also, skim the related work section (if possible).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The related work section aims to highlight work done by others that somehow ties in with the author(s) work. It may be useful to read it but if you're not familiar with the literature, it is sometimes very hard to understand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read the paper but skip the math
rubrics_metrics.description: Read the paper but skip the math.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: On a first/early pass, focus on the prose and skip dense mathematical sections; return to the math later if you want deeper understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read the whole thing but skip parts that don't make sense
rubrics_metrics.description: Read the whole thing but skip the parts that don't make sense: great research means we're publishing things at the boundaries of our knowledge and understanding. He also explained that when you read papers (even the most influential ones), you'll find maybe some parts that is much less used or it doesn't make sense. Consequently, it's fine if you read a paper and some of it doesn't make sense (it's not unusual), it's okay to skim it initially. Unless, you're trying to master it, then spend more time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tolerate partial understanding; not every part of a paper will be sensible or correct, and that is normal at the boundary of knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Answer four comprehension questions
rubrics_metrics.description: When you read a paper, try to answer the following questions: What did the author(s) try to accomplish? What were the key elements of the approach? What can you use yourself? What other references do you want to follow?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you can answer these questions, hopefully, that will reflect that you have a good understanding of the paper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rederive the math from scratch
rubrics_metrics.description: To understand the math in papers more deeply: Try to rederive it from scratch. Although, it takes some time but it's a very good practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice coding: download open-source code and reimplement from scratch
rubrics_metrics.description: To practice Coding: Download open-source code (if you can find it) and run it. Reimplement from scratch: if you can do this, that's a strong sign that you have really understood the algorithm in hand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learn steadily rather than intensively
rubrics_metrics.description: The most important thing to keep on learning and getting better is to learn more steadily rather than having a focus-intensive activity. It's better to read two papers a week for the next year than cramming everything over a short period of time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop a habit of reading research papers (maybe 2 papers a week as a start).

rubrics_metrics.name: Build a T-shaped knowledge base
rubrics_metrics.description: A very common pattern for successful machine learning engineers, strong job candidates, is to develop a T-shaped knowledge base. Meaning to have a broad understanding of many different topics in AI and very deep understanding in at least one area.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Horizontal piece is built through courses and reading research papers; vertical piece is built through related projects, open-source contributions, research and internships.
